title: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
hook: no pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour creation began; only the Creator knows (Japji 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 21. Your line was teerath tap: five good deeds, and the pilgrimage place within. Today, the same stanza asks the oldest question there is. Day one hundred ninety-six.

A week's end, so look back. Nanak the lowly, standing among the fools he named. Asankh naav, countless names. Through letters, the Name. Bhareeai hath, dirty hands. As you sow. Teerath tap. Now, a question. A kid at the dinner table asks: when did the world start? What day? What time? The adults look at each other. Someone mentions the Big Bang. Someone else says it depends who you ask. Everybody's guessing. Pauri 21 asks that exact question, very precisely, and then gives an answer that's both humble and bold.
screen: `THE WEEK: LOWLY, LETTERS, SOWING.` → `WHEN DID THE WORLD START?` → `EVERYBODY'S GUESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's how the question is asked, in paraphrase. What was that moment, what was the hour? What lunar day, what day of the week? What season, what month, when the form of the world came to be? It's like filling out a birth certificate for the universe. Then Guru Nanak goes around the room of his day. The pandits, the Hindu scholars, didn't find the time; if they had, it would be written in the Puranas. The qazis, the Muslim judges and scholars, didn't find the moment; if they had, they would have written it down. The yogi doesn't know the day or the weekday. No one knows the season or the month. And then the answer, in the original: jaa kartaa sirathee kau saaje aape jaanai soee. The Maker who shaped creation, He alone knows. Notice how even-handed it is. Pandits, qazis, yogis, the learned people of every group Guru Nanak knew. It doesn't mock any of them. It simply says: this is beyond all of us. The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: how can I speak of it, how praise it, how describe it, how know it? Everyone speaks, each trying to be wiser than the next. Great is the Master, great is His Name. And whoever thinks they're something on their own won't be honored in the end. So the lesson isn't anti-knowledge. Sikhs value learning; Japji itself is full of it. It's about the edge of knowledge, and the honesty to stand there and say: I don't know, and the Maker does.
screen: `WHAT HOUR, WHAT DAY, WHAT MONTH?` · `NO PANDIT, QAZI OR YOGI KNOWS.` · `THE MAKER ALONE KNOWS.` · `THE HONESTY TO SAY I DON'T KNOW.` · then, large: `ONLY THE MAKER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been pretending to know, or worrying because you don't: how something will turn out, why something happened, what someone else is thinking. Hold it for a moment. Then, quietly, say to yourself: I don't know. Notice what happens in your body when you say it. Some tightness might loosen. Breathe with that, and let not knowing be allowed. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 21. No pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour the world began. The Maker who shaped creation alone knows.
Your line: only the maker knows. Today, say I don't know out loud, once, about something you really don't, and let that be fine. Day one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Pauri 21 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; many Sikhs quote its lines on the pandits, qazis and yogis to say that the beginning of creation is known only to the Creator.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kartaa, the Maker, the Creator; in Pauri 21, the only one who knows when creation began.

trapdoor: what you thought: a question about the date of creation.
what it means: the beginning is beyond every scholar's reach; the Maker alone knows, and honesty admits it.

what a scholar hears: the stanza names the learned of Guru Nanak's world, pandit, qazi and jogi, evenly; the question lists vela, vakhat, thit, vaar, rut and maah, every unit of Indian time-reckoning.
